claims.text: Chemical short-range order typically suppresses lattice thermal conductivity in concentrated refractory high-entropy alloys relative to a random solid solution.
MoNbTaW can be compared in random-solid-solution and SRO-equilibrated states.
The relevant initial MoNbTaW state is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Annealing between 600 K and 1000 K can induce SRO without causing precipitation or phase separation.
An SRO state in MoNbTaW can be equilibrated at 800 K.
PDF or APT measurements can confirm the proposed SRO state through an SRO parameter alpha greater than zero.
SRO creates diffuse antiphase boundaries and local potential-energy fluctuations.
SRO produces a rugged local energy landscape that acts as a set of phonon-scattering centers.
Phonon scattering in the random solid solution is dominated by mass variance and lattice distortion.
SRO makes the local chemical environment non-random.
Phonons propagating through ordered clusters encounter an energetic cost analogous to the cost of creating diffuse antiphase boundaries during dislocation motion.
Chemical ordering adds a phonon-scattering channel, particularly for phonons whose wavelengths are comparable to the SRO correlation length.
The additional scattering increases the phonon scattering rate, reduces phonon mean free path, and lowers lattice thermal conductivity.
SRO hinders screw-dislocation motion in MoNbTaW, and this effect weakens as temperature rises.
The SRO-equilibrated alloy will have 10% to 30% lower lattice thermal conductivity than the random solid solution.
A typical MoNbTaW alloy will decrease from approximately 15 W/m·K to 10–13 W/m·K at 300 K after SRO formation.
The suppression of lattice thermal conductivity will be strongest between 300 K and 800 K.
Above the order-disorder transition temperature, SRO vanishes and thermal conductivity returns to the random-solid-solution baseline.
At sufficiently low annealing temperatures, kinetic limitations may prevent SRO formation.
Long-range precipitation introduces a distinct precipitate or grain-boundary scattering regime that may dominate over SRO effects.
